stem: A 5-year-old child was well until suddenly developing wheeze while playing with small toys. They have a persistent unilateral wheeze, reduced air entry on the right, and are not improving after inhaled salbutamol. Chest x-ray shows right-sided hyperinflation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The combination of sudden onset wheeze in an otherwise well child, poor response to bronchodilator, persistent unilateral chest findings, and focal hyperinflation on x-ray is most consistent with inhaled foreign body. Foreign body aspiration may present with focal wheeze or decreased breath sounds, and a normal or non-specific chest x-ray does not exclude it. Bronchiolitis is usually an illness of infants, asthma is typically recurrent and bronchodilator-responsive, and croup causes upper-airway barky cough and stridor rather than isolated lower-airway wheeze.

citations.title: Clinical Practice Guidelines: Foreign bodies inhaled

rationale: This is the safest and most clinically relevant interpretation of the fragment. Inhaled foreign body is the best answer because Australian paediatric guidance highlights persistent focal wheeze/decreased breath sounds and unilateral hyperinflation as key clues, and advises a high index of suspicion even when examination or x-ray findings are not definitive. The age and abrupt onset also fit aspiration more than bronchiolitis, croup, or asthma.

optionExplanations.A: Acute bronchitis may cause cough and wheeze, but it does not usually cause sudden unilateral wheeze with focal hyperinflation
optionExplanations.B: Bronchiolitis is typically seen in younger infants and usually presents with diffuse wheeze/crackles rather than a focal unilateral chest sign
optionExplanations.C: Correct: sudden onset, unilateral wheeze, reduced air entry, poor bronchodilator response, and hyperinflation strongly suggest an inhaled foreign body
optionExplanations.D: Asthma commonly causes bilateral wheeze and usually improves with salbutamol; a persistent focal chest sign should prompt another diagnosis
optionExplanations.E: Croup is an upper-airway condition causing barky cough and stridor, not focal lower-airway wheeze

evidenceSources.title: Clinical Practice Guidelines: Foreign bodies inhaled
evidenceSources.supports: Persistent focal wheeze or decreased breath sounds, sudden onset symptoms, and hyperinflation distal to obstruction are consistent with inhaled foreign body; normal exam or x-ray does not exclude it

evidenceSources.title: Clinical Practice Guidelines: Acute asthma
evidenceSources.supports: Persistent asymmetry on auscultation may indicate inhaled foreign body rather than asthma

evidenceSources.title: Clinical Practice Guidelines: Cough
evidenceSources.supports: Sudden onset without viral prodrome or after choking may suggest foreign body inhalation; dry wheeze is more typical of asthma

evidenceSources.title: Clinical Practice Guidelines: Bronchiolitis
evidenceSources.supports: Bronchiolitis is primarily an illness of infants and is less consistent with a sudden focal wheeze in a 5-year-old

answerRecovery.notes: Normalized malformed fragment into a single-best-answer question while preserving the original intended clinical concept. Existing options A-E were usable; F and G were discarded as stem fragments.
